From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. After the service, Legion members, RCMP, Sea Cadets, Air Cadets and youth organizations included Cubs, Scouts, Voyageurs, Guides and Brownies paraded to the cenotaph for wreath-laying, before returning to the Legion hall to lay wreaths at its cairn. items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. tribunal overturns $100,000 fine against X over intimate image
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal has overturned a $100,000 penalty against social media platform X for failing to delete an intimate image posted without a woman’s consent, ruling that blocking access to it in Canada was a reasonable step under provincial law. The tribunal said the law did not make X liable after it blocked Canadian access to the image, which remained available outside Canada. The decision reversed a September 2025 penalty for failing to comply with an order to delete it. The tribunal accepted X’s argument that requiring worldwide removal could interfere with other countries’ legal systems and cited a 2024 Australian case as persuasive but not binding. Outgoing B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma criticized X’s refusal to remove the image and said governments may need to strengthen laws or pursue legal action. The tribunal also rejected X’s request to require the complainant to pay more than US$100,000 in legal fees.

The Supreme Court of Canada began hearing a challenge Monday to the federal ban on more than 2,500 types of firearms the government classifies as assault-style weapons. The appeal follows two lower-court defeats for gun owners, advocacy groups and businesses challenging cabinet’s authority to prohibit the guns through regulations. The ban includes some firearms used for hunting and sport shooting. Federal lawyers argue cabinet acted reasonably to address public-safety risks, while appellants say the regulations exceeded the authority Parliament granted and failed to account for lawful sporting and hunting uses. The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

OpenAI has begun offering GPT-6 Cyber, a model designed to find and test software vulnerabilities, to a limited group of approved customers in its Daybreak Red security program. The company says researchers used it to identify 81 previously unknown, high-severity flaws in Mozilla Firefox and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, 588 of them previously unknown. Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox issues; OpenAI says it sent Linux maintainers 304 critical findings with proposed patches. OpenAI rates the model “Critical” for cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework, up from “High” for its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber. On the company’s ExploitGym benchmark, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%, compared with 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. OpenAI says the model stayed within authorized testing scope in 99.93% of tests without a deployment safety prompt and 100% of tests with one. The model’s exploit-development abilities can support security testing or be used in attacks. OpenAI says it added safeguards including account and network controls, monitoring and reviews of high-risk activity. It plans to expand access to approved Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Researchers identify new dinosaur genus from fossil found in England in 2001

🎨 ✏️

Paleontologists have classified a fossil found in a Surrey clay quarry in 2001 as Paludohadros proudlovii, a previously unknown genus and species of plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 125 million years ago. The four-legged animal was about 5 metres long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons, but its bones indicate it had not reached adulthood. The fossil was donated to London’s Natural History Museum, where it remained for years before a detailed comparison with other iguanodontians revealed distinguishing features. The identification also helped researchers identify fossils collected from the same quarry in the 1950s as belonging to the newly named dinosaur. The research, led by Ricardo Sacamoto, a PhD student at the Natural History Museum and the University of São Paulo, was published in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology on Oct. 26, 2026. Sacamoto plans to continue examining the museum’s iguanodontian collection.

items.title: [annahar.com] Scientists identify 66-million-year-old dinosaur adapted to eating fruit
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers identified Infernogallus jamesi, a turkey-sized, toothless dinosaur that lived about 66 million years ago and appears to have specialized in eating fruit and other soft plants. Its fossils, including a nearly complete skeleton, came from Montana and North Dakota. Its beak and jaw were adapted for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur with evidence of a specialized fruit diet. Paleontologist Greg Funston of Stony Brook University, lead author of the study published in Nature Communications, said the dinosaur's anatomy suggests a specialized feeding method. The researchers say it may have eaten berries and fleshy fruits; whether it helped spread large-seeded plants remains uncertain and requires more evidence.

🎨 ✏️

OpenAI says a mid-October campaign using its GPT-6 Cyber model generated 948 working Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploits at an average API cost of $1,279 each; 588 of the targeted flaws were previously unknown. The exploits could let someone with ordinary local access gain root privileges, and OpenAI says it sent Linux maintainers 304 critical findings with proposed patches. The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre warned that AI tools are accelerating vulnerability discovery and that organizations must adapt their patching and testing processes. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on Nov. 5 for a limited group of approved customers in its Daybreak Red program, which supports authorized advanced security testing. The model also helped identify 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox flaws; Mozilla has begun releasing fixes. OpenAI says the model stayed within its assigned scope in 99.93% of tests without an additional deployment safety prompt, but The Register reported that OpenAI declined to detail the cases in which it crossed that boundary. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant, where it identified two previously unknown flaws in engineering software that handles protective-relay data, according to Cybersecurity News. OpenAI has added a dedicated access group for approved critical-infrastructure defenders and says it is expanding access to GPT-6 Cyber across approved Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] WMO says powerful El Niño likely to persist through February 2027
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Hackers used employee access and wallet authorization to steal $6.34 billion from Binance
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said attackers spent months compromising employee computers, then used stolen credentials and a wallet authorization mechanism to bypass normal transfer controls and steal about $6.34 billion on Oct. 29. The FBI attributed the operation to North Korean-linked hackers; North Korea denied responsibility. Binance traced the intrusion to a June infection through a tampered Homebrew installer, followed in September by a fake recruitment process that led another engineer to run a malicious coding assignment. The malware replaced a legitimate development component and evaded endpoint security. By Oct. 20, attackers were using a compromised computer and an internal AI tool to access two wallet engineers’ systems. On Oct. 29, attackers used a stolen deployment token to run a script and exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization feature. Binance said the wallet’s multiparty-computation design meant no single private key could immediately revoke the authorization, requiring it to develop a special procedure. The exchange said it cleared the delegation at 00:10 UTC on Oct. 30. Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool and commissioned independent cybersecurity experts to review the breach.
